summary: Algonquin Park's last standing fire tower, built 1956; lightning burned its wooden cupola in 2010 or 2011 and the steel frame remains.

facts.design: Metal (steel) frame tower with a wooden cupola at the top
facts.status_note: Only the metal frame stands; the wooden cupola burned.

access.note: Inside Algonquin Provincial Park. Firelookout.ca says the site is accessible via hiking.

visit.trail_note: Reached on foot, up a steep hill from the ranger cabin. The park's Fire Tower Trail at the visitor centre is a separate 200 m round trip with a replica cupola, not this tower.

events.note: Park sources say the fire ranger's cabin, boathouse and tower were all built in 1956.
Park says the tower was used for fire detection up to the mid-1970s. 1975 is approximate; the source gives only 'mid-1970s'.
Firelookout.ca says lightning hit the wooden shelter at the top in May 2011 and the fire burned it. The park's 2013 release gives 2010 for the same loss.

evidence.quote: Big Crow Lake Fire Tower was a tower located within Algonquin Park however in 2011 the tower burned down leaving only the frame left.

evidence.supports: Little remains beyond the base and metal frame; site is accessible by hiking
evidence.quote: Currently, the site is accessible via hiking but little remains apart from the base and metal frame.

evidence.quote: Lightning struck the wooden shelter atop the tower in May 2011 and it subsequently burned the entire structure.

evidence.quote: Only the metal tower is left standing and charred wood can be found at the base of the tower.

corrections.why: The 2011 event is a lightning fire that burned the wooden top of the tower. The burned event type describes it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Firelookout.ca dates the lightning fire to May 2011. The park's 2013 news release says the cupola was burnt in 2010. The story gives the register's 2011 and reports the park's 2010.

One Firelookout.ca entry says the tower burned down to its frame. The other says the fire burned the wooden shelter and that only the metal tower is left. Both agree the metal frame survives, so the story says the top burned and the frame stands.

sources.title: New Fire Tower Trail Coming to Algonquin Park Visitor Centre

notes_for_editor: Brief local unit 'Nipissing District' is kept as given; the older Canada Lookouts index files the site under 'Pembrooke District - Algonquin Park', which the story does not repeat. The 1956 date is park-sourced and the 1975 staffing year is approximate. The 'steel' description comes from the park's Fire Tower Trail page and the metal frame from Firelookout.ca; no photo with a licence was found. The Fire Tower Trail at the visitor centre is a replica, not this tower, and the story says so.
